name: Mohawk

lead: A mohawk is a haircut in which the sides of the head are shaved or cut short and a longer strip is left down the centre. It is a statement style associated with punk, military and sport subcultures.

It changes the head's outline and draws the eye upward and along the centre line. Looksmaxxing forum members treat it as a trendy, high-risk-high-reward style; there is no research on its effect on attractiveness.

paras: Barbers shave or fade the sides and leave the centre long; the centre may be spiked or styled upright. A fauxhawk is a milder version that leaves the sides unshaved.
No health risks from the cut itself. The main consideration is that it is a strong look that suits some contexts better than others, and grow-out takes time.

angle.text: The cut reshapes the head's outline and can add height and edge to a hairstyle. It is chosen as a statement look.

lead: A mohawk (called a mohican in British English) is a hairstyle in which both sides of the head are shaved or cut very short and a strip of longer hair is left running from the forehead to the nape.[1] People choose it to change the outline of the head: the centre strip adds height on top, draws the eye up and along the midline, and puts the sides of the skull and the ears on display.

Wikipedia traces similar cuts across thousands of years, from Herodotus's account of the Macai of northern Libya and the Pawnee of Nebraska and Kansas to 16th-century Ukrainian Cossacks, and notes that World War II paratroopers revived it and that it became tied to punk in the 1970s.[1] Softer versions such as the fauxhawk, which leaves the sides unshaved, bring the same upward shape into everyday settings.[1]

Looksmax.org users discuss the style as trendy and bold, and note its popularity among athletes such as BJJ competitors.[2][3] No published study has examined how a mohawk affects perceived attractiveness.
infobox: Fauxhawk, reverse mohawk, euro-hawk, liberty spike

paras: The classic mohawk shaves both sides and leaves a narrow, upright strip of longer hair from forehead to nape.[1] The centre can be worn flat, spiked, backcombed or styled into a point.[1]

Wikipedia lists a family of variants. The reverse mohawk (also called a nohawk or hawkmo) shaves the centre and keeps hair on either side, and early examples include wrestler Road Warrior Hawk and Peter Gabriel on tour in 1973.[1] The fauxhawk uses a shorter central strip without shaving the sides, and was known as the Hoxton fin in 1990s London before a 2000s revival.[1] The euro-hawk is a fauxhawk with longer centre hair that can be combed over the shorter sides, and the ponyhawk is built from a row of ponytails.[1] Others include the deathhawk (backcombed, worn by goths), the dreadhawk, the Chelsea hawk and the liberty spike mohawk.[1]

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: Barbers describe the cut in general terms as a contrast of lengths: short or faded sides against a longer centre. This makes the head look taller and narrower from the front and draws attention to the face and the line of the centre strip. A fauxhawk achieves a milder version of that lift while keeping the sides in place, and a fade on the sides can be made gradual or sharp depending on the look.
Because the shaved sides are cut short, the style needs regular trims to stay crisp, and it grows out into a longer cut over time.[1]

Wikipedia states that the name's link to the Mohawk people comes mainly from Hollywood, particularly the 1939 film Drums Along the Mohawk, whereas Haudenosaunee men historically plucked a patch of hair rather than shaving it.[1] The article adds that the term mohican gained currency in the UK after a 1971 BBC adaptation of The Last of the Mohicans.[1]

Earlier or parallel examples cited include the Macai described by Herodotus, the Pawnee, and Ukrainian Cossacks who shaved the head but for a central strip called an oseledets or chupryna.[1] In 1944-era World War II, paratroopers of the 17th and 101st Airborne wore the cut, and jazz musicians such as Sonny Rollins wore it in the early 1950s.[1] In the 1970s the style became associated with punk subculture, and wearers listed by Wikipedia include Mr. T, Joe Strummer, Flea, David Beckham and Neymar.[1]

A looksmax.org thread asks whether to get a mohawk because it seems trendy; replies are joking and mixed.[2] Another thread asks why BJJ competitors often wear mohawks or shaved sides; replies suggest practicality or intimidation, without sources.[3]
Wikipedia records Joseph Grisamore as holder of the tallest full mohawk at 108 cm, and Kazuhiro Watanabe as holder of the tallest mohican at 113.5 cm.[1]
